column2: A slate reads nine. Someone is rewriting it as ten. Glance at it mid-stroke, and you might read nine, or ten, or, Lamport says, two thousand four hundred ninety-six.
Could computers take turns safely with memory like that? In nineteen seventy-three, that was considered impossible.
Two programs, running at once, share a scoreboard that reads forty-one. Programmers call it x, and write x equals x plus one. It isn't an equation. It means make x one bigger.
That's two steps. Read the score, then write it back plus one.
Here's one unlucky order. Both read forty-one, and both write forty-two. Two points scored, one counted.
Draw every order at once, as staircases from corner to corner. There are six. How many lose a point?
Four. Exactly the ones through the middle, where both have read and neither has written. The fix has to wall off the middle.
Counting orders isn't measuring chances. Each program usually runs both steps back to back. But a fix has to work in every order.
The fix seems obvious. Only one program at a time may touch the scoreboard. Call that stretch of code the room.
Put a sign on the door. Check that it says vacant, flip it to occupied, and go in.
Does the sign work?
No. Both read vacant before either flips it. Of the fourteen orders, eight put both in the room at once.
Dijkstra posed the problem properly in nineteen sixty-five. Never two in the room. Someone who stops outside the room can't hold up anyone else. And fast or slow, it still works.
A year later, Donald Knuth asked for more. Everyone who wants in gets in eventually.

Hardware usually cheats, with a magic sign you can check and flip in one motion. Dijkstra showed that ordinary signs are enough, several of them used cleverly, as long as nobody can catch one halfway through a flip.
Now a harder question. What if a glance can catch a sign mid-flip, as a blur? Hold that thought.

In nineteen seventy-four, Leslie Lamport found an answer. Picture a bakery. Take a number, and the lowest ticket is served next. From now on, each program is a customer, and being served means going into the room.
But a ticket machine is shared. Two customers pressing at once could get the same ticket, just like the lost point. It would need a room of its own.
So each customer gets her own slate, and only she writes on it. A zero means not in line.
To take a ticket, read every other slate, one at a time, and write one more than the biggest. Blue reads three, zero, zero, two. What does she write?
Four. Then she waits until nobody with a smaller ticket is still in line. Here that's Pink, with two, then Green, with three, then Blue.
Whoever is in the room plays their own tune, so only one tune sounds at a time.
No shared ticket machine. Nobody ever writes on anyone else's slate.
Can two customers get the same ticket?
Yes. Before anyone is served, Purple and Teal read at the same moment. Both see four as the biggest, and both write five.

Our rule only waits for smaller tickets, so both can end up in the room at once. Change the rule to wait for anyone with a smaller or equal ticket, and they both wait, bowing to each other forever. After you. No, after you.

The fix is a tie-breaker. Pair each ticket with its customer number, and compare tickets first. Only if they're equal, compare customer numbers, the way a dictionary checks the second letter only when the first letters match. Purple is three and Teal is four, so Purple goes first.
Put every pair on a grid, ticket across and customer number up, and sweep column by column. Blue is customer number one. Does she go before Pink and Green?

No. Blue's four still waits for Pink's two and Green's three. The customer number only breaks ties. The room always takes the smallest pair of everyone holding a ticket, so it goes Pink, Green, Blue, Purple, then Teal.
There's a sneakier crack. Blue reads Green's slate, sees zero, and decides on ticket one. But she hasn't written it yet.
Green takes ticket one, checks Blue's slate, sees zero, which means not in line, and walks in.
Then Blue writes her one, sees a tie, wins it on her lower customer number, and walks in too. Both in the room.
The fix is a flag that says, I'm choosing, don't judge me yet. Raise it before reading, and lower it after writing. Before comparing with someone, wait until their flag is down.
Same unlucky order, now with flags. What does Green do this time?
She sees Blue's flag up, and waits.
Without flags, two customers visiting once have twenty-eight orders, and four put both in the room. With flags, there are three hundred twenty-two, and not one does.
The time your flag is up is your choosing time. Unlike the door sign, the flag isn't a lock. Nobody waits to raise their own, and many can be up at once.
So two customers can still choose at once. The flag just shows everyone who's choosing, and the tie-breaker settles equal tickets.
Now take three customers. The square becomes a cube. How many orders are there now?
Over two billion. And not one of them puts two in the room.
Here's one full run, fast.
Purple and Green arrive together, and both choose ticket one. Purple finishes first and finds Green's flag still up, so she waits. Without the flag, she'd have read Green's unwritten ticket as zero.
Next, Teal sees two ones. What ticket does she take?
Two. And the tie between Purple and Green goes to Green, customer two, ahead of Purple, customer three.

Green goes in first. Blue, customer number one, arrives late and takes three. Green is out before Blue checks her, so Blue only waits for Purple, then Teal. Green gets back in line and takes four, behind Blue.
Five visits, five points on the scoreboard, none lost. Who gets served first follows the grid exactly.
Why can two customers never be in the room at once? Picture Blue inside, and Green holding a ticket.
Fact one. If Blue finished choosing before Green started, and still holds that ticket, then Green's ticket is bigger. Green saw Blue's.
Fact two. If Blue is in the room, every other ticket holder has a bigger pair than hers. Why is that true?
Take the last time Blue checked Green's flag, the check that let her through. Where could Green have been?
There are three places. Not yet choosing. Blue had already finished choosing, so by fact one, Green's ticket will be bigger.
In the middle of choosing. Then Green's flag was up, and that check wouldn't have let Blue through.
Finished choosing. Then Blue had read Green's real ticket, and went in only because her pair was smaller. Either way, Green's pair is bigger. And that's fact two.
Now suppose both were in the room. Then fact two says each one's pair is smaller than the other's. Like me being taller than you, and you taller than me. Impossible.
A computer search agrees, over every order, up to four customers, as long as tickets stay small. Only the proof covers every case.
Remember the slate caught mid-stroke? Rewrite oh-nine as ten one digit at a time, and a glance in between reads nineteen, or zero zero.
Lamport went further. A glance during a write may return any number the slate could hold. Even two thousand four hundred ninety-six.
Twelve years later he named memory like that safe. A funny name, since it's the least safe kind.
Back to the proof picture. Let every slate and every flag flicker while it's written. Does the proof ever trust a glance at a slate while it's being written?
Never. It trusts only two glances at slates. Green reading Blue's finished ticket, and Blue reading Green's finished ticket. Nobody was writing either slate.
A glance that catches garbage, say seven, just makes a customer take eight and wait longer.
And a glance that catches Blue's old zero mid-write lets Green straight in. Is that dangerous?

No. Blue's flag is up while she takes a ticket, and Green had already seen it down. So Blue raised it after Green finished choosing. That's fact one the other way round, so Blue's ticket will be bigger, and she waits.
Lamport noticed that the algorithm survives garbage only after writing the proof. In his words, the read may return any arbitrary value. His colleague Anatol Holt refused to believe it.

One caution, from Lamport himself. Find the biggest ticket by reading each slate exactly once. The obvious way reads a slate twice, once to compare and once to copy, and a flicker between them can break it.
So, could computers take turns safely with memory like that? Yes.
It's also fair. Finish choosing your ticket before I start choosing mine, and you're served first. If we choose at the same time, either of us may go first.

As long as everyone in the room comes out, and nobody stalls for good with a raised flag or a ticket, whoever holds the smallest pair gets through. Once you've taken your ticket, each other customer can get ahead of you at most once. So nobody waits forever.
The price is that tickets keep growing while somebody is always in line. They reset only when the bakery empties.
Lamport did the sum. At one customer a millisecond, how big do the tickets get in a year?
Up to about thirty-one and a half billion, one per millisecond. That's too big for a thirty-two bit slate. Like the odometer, it could roll over in under two months.
A sixty-four bit slate lasts centuries, even at a billion tickets a second. That sum assumes a glance never returns more than was really written. One huge glance makes the tickets after it huge too.
And it isn't cheap. Even alone, a customer makes three reads for every other customer. One customer frozen while choosing stalls everyone.
The proof is right, but run as written on your laptop, the algorithm can fail. A finished write isn't always seen by every later read.
Your laptop has several processors, called cores. Picture each one running a customer. Each core drops its writes in an outbox and keeps going.
Both customers raise their flags and write their tickets, into their outboxes. Then each checks the other's flag and slate. What does she see?
No flag, and no ticket. Both walk in, while the real flags and slates still say nobody is even choosing.

The fix is a fence. Wait until your outbox is delivered before reading anyone else's slate. On an Intel or AMD chip, two fences each time you enter are enough, one after raising your flag, and one after lowering it.
Arm chips, like the ones in recent Macs, shuffle more than an outbox does. Others can see your flag come down before your ticket lands, which is chapter five's bug again.

For programmers, the easy, correct way everywhere is sequentially consistent atomic reads and writes. Acquire and release are not enough here, because this needs your write to land before your next read.
In practice, people use the hardware's magic signs, which check and flip in one motion. So does the bakery still run anywhere?

Yes. Code that Arm itself publishes uses it while a core wakes up, before its fast memory is switched on. Until then, the magic signs aren't guaranteed to work, so the core takes a ticket, bakery style.

And its trick of taking a ticket bigger than any you've seen, with customer numbers to break ties, reappears in how Lamport later ordered events across whole networks. It's in the ballot numbers of Paxos too, the method that keeps copies of a database agreeing.
Lamport says he didn't invent the bakery algorithm. He discovered it. It just seemed to come out of thin air, and perhaps, he says, that's why he's proudest of it.
